THE   MACMILLAN  COMPANY 

Publishers  64-66  Fifth  Avenue  New  York 


BY  THE  SAME  AUTHOR 

The  Supreme  Court  and  the  Constitution 

Cloth,  i2mo,  $1.00  net;  postpaid,  $i.o8 

Did  the  framers  of  the  federal  Constitution  intend  that  the 
Supreme  Court  should  pass  upon  the  constitutionality  of  acts 
of  Congress?  The  emphatic  negative  recently  given  to  this 
question  by  legal  writers  of  respectable  authority  has  put  the 
sanction  of  some  guild  members  on  the  popular  notion  that  the 
nullification  of  statutes  by  the  federal  judiciary  is  warranted 
neither  by  the  letter  nor  by  the  spirit  of  the  supreme  law  of 
the  land  and  is,  therefore,  rank  usurpation.  In  "  The  Supreme 
Court  and  the  Constitution"  Professor  Charles  A.  Beard  con- 
siders these  statements  which  have  been  made  by  various  au- 
thorities in  regard  to  the  usurpation  by  the  Supreme  Court  of 
powers  not  granted  in  the  Constitution.  He  hangs  together 
documentary  evidence  to  indicate  that  the  majority  of  the  lead- 
ing members  of  the  Constitutional  Convention  were  in  favor 
of  a  judicial  interpretation  of  the  Constitution.  Considerable 
matter  is  cited  from  "  The  Fathers  "  and  also  reference  is  made 
to  other  publications  on  the  history  of  the  Constitution.  The 
book  is  a  concise  one,  leaving  out  all  extraneous  matter  and 
confining  itself  to  the  significant  points  at  issue. 


"The  book  is  by  far  the  most  valuable  contribution  that 
has  yet  been  made  to  this  intensely  interesting  subject."  — 
Annals  of  the  American  Academy. 

"  For  a  brief  and  quite  impersonal  piece  of  historical  re- 
search the  book  is  eminently  readable  and  should  find  a  wider 
audience  than  that  of  lawyers  and  historians  alone." — The 
Independent. 

THE  MACMILLAN  COMPANY 

Publishers  64-66  Fifth  Avenue  New  York 


Contemporary  American  History 

1877-1913 
By   CHARLES    A.   BEARD 

Associate  Professor  of  Politics  in  Columbia  University 

This  volume  covers  the  history  of  the  United  States  from 
the  close  of  the  Reconstruction  Period  to  the  inauguration  of 
President  Wilson.  Although  the  work  is  historical  in  character 
it  is  written  from  the  point  of  view  of  contemporary  affairs 
and  designed  to  furnish  a  background  for  the  leading  issues 
of  current  politics.  Such  matters  as  the  negro  question,  the 
industrial  revolution,  capitalism  and  socialism,  free  silver  and 
populism,  direct  government,  woman  suffrage,  the  growth  of 
judicial  review,  new  nationalism,  imperialism,  the  labor  move- 
ment, Mr.  Roosevelt's  policies,  the  progressive  movement,  and 
"  the  new  freedom  "  are  treated  in  a  historical  manner,  with 
a  view  to  placing  the  leading  facts  before  students  and  en- 
gaging their  interest.  A  carefully  selected  bibliography  affords 
a  handy  guide  to  additional  reading. 

This  is  the  only  work  of  moderate  compass  covering  the 
period  and  will  meet  the  needs  of  those  alert  teachers  who 
endeavor  to  link  their  historical  instruction  with  the  living 
present.  It  will  also  make  feasible  the  establishment  of  the 
new  course  of  instruction  in  contemporary  history  and  politics 
which  is  now  demanded  in  so  many  quarters.  Although  de- 
signed primarily  as  a  guide  for  a  college  course,  it  may  be 
used  with  profit  as  a  collateral  work  in  high  school  courses  in 
American  history  and  politics.  The  absence  of  the  earmarks 
of  the  textbook  will  also  make  the  volume  acceptable  to  the 
general  reader. 


THE   MACMILLAN  COMPANY 

Publishers  64-66  Fifth  Avenue  New  York 


The  Governments  of  Europe 

By  FREDERIC   AUSTIN    OGG,   Ph.D. 

Assistant  Professor  of  History  in  Simmons  College 

Cloth,  8vo,  646  pp.  +  index,  $3.00  net 

Of  the  thirty-four  chapters  in  this  volume  on  the  Governments  of 
Europe,  eight  are  devoted  to  Great  Britain,  six  to  Germany,  four  to 
France,  four  to  Austria-Hungary,  three  to  Italy,  two  to  Switzerland, 
and  one  each  to  Holland,  Belgium,  Denmark,  Sweden,  Norway,  Spain, 
and  Portugal.  The  author  has  confined  himself  largely  to  a  descrip- 
tion of  the  governments  of  to-day,  although  he  has  given  such  brief 
accounts  of  the  historical  origin  and  development  of  the  present  con- 
stitutions as  are  necessary  to  enable  the  student  to  acquire  a  sound 
and  comprehensive  view  of  the  organization  and  administration  of  the 
existing  governments.  So  far  as  is  possible  in  the  limits  of  a  single 
volume,  the  author  has  treated  the  federal,  state,  and  local  govern- 
ments, the  executive,  legislative,  and  judicial  branches  thereof,  and  the 
organizations,  doctrines,  and  workings  of  the  political  parties.  Com- 
parisons of  the  governments  of  the  different  countries  have  been  made 
when  and  only  when  they  will  be  found  of  real  interest  and  value  to 
the  student.  The  book  will  be  found  especially  adapted  to  use  as  a 
text  in  college  courses  on  Comparative,  Constitutional,  or  European 
Governments. 

"  Professor  Ogg's  book  will  prove  serviceable  for  the  general  reader 
who  wishes  clear  and  concise  accounts  of  how  government  is  adminis- 
tered in  the  European  states." —  The  Dial. 

"Avery  painstaking,  comprehensive,  and  useful  compendium."  — 
American  Review  of  Reviews. 

"The  present  volume  is  one  of  the  most  elaborate  and  best  we  have 
had  the  pleasure  of  examining."  —  Education.
